stories.title_en: Alarming Talk Goads a Man Back to Gambling

paragraphs.en: Zhang Shisheng of Juxi was a pampered son of wealth. His father had amassed ten thousand taels and divided them equally among Shisheng and his brothers; the fields and gardens were fertile, and the sons lived at ease on a ready-made estate. When the father died, just as Wanli coins were first coming into circulation, swindlers lured Shisheng into gambling. A greenhorn from a rich house, he saw only the bold drinking and swagger of the gambling rooms—a wild and carefree life that suited him. How would he know that money is to be treasured? Within a few months he had lost several hundred taels of silver, yet he still went on gambling happily, with no thought of stopping.

In the village lived a man named Chen Rongyi, whom Shisheng's late father had employed as a trusted household agent. Humble as he was, he possessed a loyal and upright heart and could not bear to watch Shisheng being led astray by swindlers. So he prepared a fine feast and invited Shisheng alone. Over wine, he spoke slowly and at length: from beginning to end, he recounted how the father had built his fortune and exactly how he had guarded every coin and every grain of rice. He praised the father's ability and sighed over his hardships; then he spoke of worldly ways, of how hard cash and rice are to come by, and of the misery of the poor who have none. At last he urged him: "It was not easy for your late father to amass such wealth. You must remember your forebears' toil and hold on to the family foundation. Whatever you do, stop gambling. True, you have already lost several hundred taels, but let bygones be bygones. Mend your ways from today, and you can still live at ease on the family fortune." Shisheng saw that Rongyi's words were earnest, and for a moment his conscience stirred. "I will do as you say," he said. "From today I swear off gambling." The next day the swindlers came for him, and sure enough he would not go. The gang was baffled; when they later learned it was Rongyi's doing, there was nothing they could do. They took counsel: "Whoever can get him gambling again, we will pool ten taels for him." A man named Chai Kun said, "I can do it." The gang sealed up ten taels of silver as the prize.

Kun found Shisheng sitting idly in a roadside pavilion. He sidled up, chatted of this and that, and then asked, “Is it true you have quit gambling?” Shisheng said it was. Kun said, “Gambling is a bad business. To see that and turn back on your own—that is the mark of a true hero. For the son of a great and wealthy house to show such sense, I honestly admire you. Only—everyone is saying it was old Rongyi who talked you into stopping. Is that really so?” Shisheng said, “It is. It was his advice.” Chai Kun sighed. “Rongyi is a low-life crook, a mere runner of errands. Is he your father or brother? Is he your uncle? What right has he to forbid you anything? You are the son of a famous family, a clever man—why take instruction from a scoundrel? If word gets around that you take orders from a low fellow, people will laugh at you behind your back and say you have no spine. In my view, you should go back for a little light gambling. After half a month or a month, quit on your own. Then people will say you stopped because you no longer cared for gambling, not because you obeyed a servant's orders. That is how a true man acts, and it brings no shame on your family's name.” Shisheng was a witless greenhorn. Hearing this smooth, false talk, he thought to himself: “True enough—if I stop now, people will call it Rongyi's achievement. Better to gamble another month and then quit on my own. Won't I stand out as a hero then?” He went straight back to the gambling rooms. Chai Kun quietly collected the gang's silver and left.

Shisheng gambled for a month, and his reckless appetite came roaring back. After that, though Rongyi spoke to him again, the words no longer got through, and in the end he gambled away the whole family fortune. All of it sprang from Chai Kun's single provocation. Fierce was the ruin it wrought.

Note: Shisheng was taken in by Chai Kun's specious nonsense and rejected Rongyi's loyal counsel, all because the man was humble and he thought it shameful to be advised by him. He did not know that Yao put questions to the common people, that Shun sought counsel from woodcutters, that the Duke of Zhou hurried out to welcome men of low rank, that Han Xin begged a plan from Li Zuoche. Emperors, kings, generals, and ministers still bent down to hear humble words like these—how can you throw away good advice because the man who gives it is low? Pity that Shisheng was a green boy who knew nothing of past or present, and so swallowed the slander without ever seeing it for what it was. Alas.

stories.title_en: A Fake Young Lord and a Courtesan Fleece a Gambler

paragraphs.en: Wang Dixi was the son of a family worth ten thousand taels. He loved gambling insatiably, and his gambling friends conspired against him so often that his whole fortune was lost. Later he scraped together what capital remained—barely three hundred taels—took a single servant, and went back to the county town to gamble. The sharps there pooled their funds and took turns at the table with him. By then Dixi's household was ruined, but his skill at gambling had grown very high: he could not beat the pack of sharps, yet they could not beat him either. For over half a month they held each other off, but no new young gentlemen came to town and there were no greenhorns to net. So Dixi went on to the prefectural city; and since no gambling den there was big enough to please him either, he went to visit the courtesan Li Xiqing.

Two or three of his gambling partners tracked him down to the house. Hearing that Dixi had gone into the brothel, they hatched a plan: "We will rope him in this way, and we can take every coin he has." The next day, waiting until Dixi had gone out to find his gambling partners, they went inside and said to Xiqing: "Dixi only likes gambling, not women; he has no rich gifts for you. Do as we tell you: first, we will send you twenty taels as a gift; afterward, from whatever we win at the table, you shall get an extra two taels per hundred." Xiqing agreed. At noon she laid out a lavish meal, and she and Dixi had drunk only a few cups when two menservants suddenly arrived bearing gifts—dazzling, splendid things, all first-rate, worth more than twenty taels. "Our young lord sends this trifling token," they said. "He will be here shortly." Xiqing looked the gifts over one by one, had them all put away, served tea to the two servants outside, then returned to the table to keep Dixi company—half delighted, half putting on a show of vexation. Dixi said, "Someone sends you rich gifts, and you look put out instead. Why?" Xiqing said, "If you had not asked, I could hardly have brought it up. These are from Young Lord Huang. Last year he gambled here and lost more than a thousand taels, and he was generous to me besides. He is due to arrive today. I beg your pardon, sir—I must go out to welcome him. Let me make it up to you with extra days of company afterward." Dixi said, "If it is a young lord, I will step out and leave the field to him." Xiqing said brightly, "With such forbearance, sir, you are a second heaven to me." Dixi made to rise, but she held him back. "Sit a while longer, it does no harm. One thing more: this man is lively and without pretensions. In a while, if the chance arises and he asks to meet you, or wants to talk here together, keep him company for me. If you lend me your worthy presence, it raises my standing too." Dixi had meant to leave the table, but the moment he heard that the young lord used to gamble here, his heart was already ten parts pleased. He kept his one servant to wait on him, drank alone in the inner room, and sent Xiqing out to receive the guest.

Presently the young lord arrived, and Xiqing served tea with an easy grace. When the usual civilities were done, the young lord got straight up, meaning to stroll into the inner rooms. Xiqing hurriedly begged him to stop. “A kinsman from elsewhere has just come a long way,” she said, “and is inside having a simple meal. I am afraid there is nowhere for him to withdraw.” The young lord laughed. “A lover is a lover—why dress him up as an outside kinsman? If he is your man, I have never been the jealous sort. What harm is there in asking him out to meet me?” He sent two servants in to invite him. When they did not come out at once, he pressed Xiqing: “You go and ask him.” Xiqing went in and brought Di Xi out. The young lord looked him over—a fine figure, no common man—and laughed, “Xiqing is a woman of taste; she really does know how to pick a fine gentleman.” He came forward and they exchanged courtesies. The banquet ordered for the courtyard had arrived; the young lord took the seat of honor, Di Xi sat facing him, and Xiqing sat at the left in attendance. All through the meal they talked and laughed, never once touching on gambling. At nightfall they called for dice to play drinking games. The young lord joked, “I only fear I don't yet know a true connoisseur of beauty when I see one.” Xiqing said, “The young lord has the dash to stake a million on a single cast, and Di Xi has the zest to shout for the winning throw and claim the prize. This poor girl is only ashamed she is no great beauty to be fond of.” The young lord said, “So Di Xi is a real player too? Tomorrow morning, what say we gamble for a small treat?” Di Xi said, “The treat is mine to offer—no need to gamble for it.” The young lord said, “A meal that costs nothing has no savor; it must be won to be worth anything.” He took the dice and threw first—nothing. Di Xi won with a single cast. The young lord raised the stake by another play and lost again. His blood was up. “Di Xi, what a hand you have! Once more, you and I, to settle win and loss.” Di Xi said, “I would not presume to reach so high, but I am game to keep you company.” The two fell to gambling, and the wins went back and forth.

By the first watch, the young lord had lost over a hundred taels, and Xiqing had already taken her cut of ten-plus taels. She gathered up the dice and said, "You have had a tiring day in the sedan chair, and the night is deep; you must go to sleep. Tomorrow, over wine at the play, we can settle the score, and perhaps show me a little favor with the cut." The young lord, having lost heavily, flew into a temper and demanded to continue. Di Xi too made a bold declaration: "If we go on, it must be a hundred taels a pile, or we stop!" The young lord produced ready silver and stacked it a hundred to the pile. Xiqing deliberately held onto the dice and refused to hand them over. The young lord flared up: "One throw only—win or lose, we are done!" Xiqing returned the dice. The young lord won on a single cast and took the hundred taels. "Another pile, same as before," he said. He won again. "All my life I have liked big stakes, never small ones. Make it two hundred a pile." Just as he was working himself into a fever, torches and a sedan chair were suddenly heard at the gate. A servant rushed in: "His Lordship is searching for you urgently; you must return at once!" The young lord said, "My luck has just turned—why spoil my run?" His next throw won another two-hundred pile. The servants pressed him as if the house were on fire. "Tomorrow I cannot come by day," the young lord said, "but at night I will surely be here." Di Xi tried to keep him, without success. Xiqing put on a stunned, witless look of fright and hurried to see him off. Then she came back and rounded on Di Xi: "No one wins forever. You had won a great deal at first; you should have known when to stop. When the young lord wanted to win it back, why did you put out even bigger piles? That is not knowing how to avoid a winning streak. A fine old hand you are—your judgment does not match a mere woman's." Di Xi said, "I have gambled away ten thousand taels in my time. What is a mere three hundred to me? What is the great matter, that you should fret and fume over it?" He stayed on at Xiqing's house for several days; when she pressed him to stay longer, he firmly declined and left.

Note: The young lord was an impostor. He first sent lavish gifts to the courtesan to make Dixi believe he was a real nobleman; everything thereafter was staged. The loaded dice had already been hidden in Xiqing's hand, which is why she snatched up the honest dice and then handed back the loaded ones, so he would suspect nothing. Three throws, three wins; once the trap was set to urge him home, who could guard against it? Yet even Dixi, a practiced hand, could not have fathomed such a cheat. In gambling, tricks breed beyond tricks. To see the snare in this story, recognize the moment, and take your hand off the table for good—that is the truly sound plan. Do not end like him, with your whole purse emptied in a single day.

stories.title_en: A Lover of Gambling Falls into Another's Trap

paragraphs.en: Xu Huasheng of Fujian, styled Hanxiu, was boastful and arrogant by nature, and he loved gambling fiercely. One day, he bought a stock of paper to sell in the capital. There was also a man named Zhang E, styled Shuzhen, who had once been rich but was ruined by gambling; he still had a few hundred taels left in his purse and had also bought paper to sell in the capital. The two were from the same county but different hometowns, lodging at the same inn. E had a scheme in mind. He often played chess with Huasheng at the inn, sometimes betting on a treat, sometimes on seasonal fruit. In truth, E's chess was strong enough to give Huasheng a chariot, but E was a lone traveler while the Xu clan was numerous. So E often lost the treat on purpose, while secretly winning over Huasheng's fellow townsmen, silencing them so they would say nothing about it. He would lose five games and win only two, yet Huasheng never guessed that E was hiding his true sharpness.

One evening, Zhang E was already asleep when Huasheng roused him to gamble for a treat. E was delighted: "Tonight is the chance." So he feigned reluctance and refused to get up. When pressed again, E said, "I will not gamble for a treat; we must gamble for silver." Sheng thought to himself, "My chess skills are superior; what do I have to fear?" He answered at once, "Even better." Unaware that he had fallen into their trap, he proceeded. Moreover, being naturally arrogant and detested by his fellow townspeople, everyone egged the wager on. E said, "First, let us weigh out the silver face to face; the loser pays immediately, no backing out. One tael per game, with two qian from each tael going to the company as a cut to cover the treat and the show." Sheng said, "Two taels is no problem." Before long, he lost several games. His blood heated, and he demanded ten taels per game. The older, steadier guests said, "No—you should stop now." The younger ones provoked him further. Sheng's blood grew hotter; he weighed out another ten taels and played on. Within a few more games, he had lost dozens of taels in total. By then, dawn was breaking. E swept the winnings into his bag and stood up. Sheng begged him to play on; E flatly refused, and the two grappled fiercely. E said, "You invited me to gamble, not I you. If I had lost to you, would you have let me off? My family had several thousand taels, and gambling emptied it. You have lost this trifling sum—why the fuss? Are you really a man? Take me to the magistrate if you like; I will not pay it back." The older guests said, "It was we who lacked the sense to stop you, leading to your ruin. But Brother Zhang is right: if he had lost to you, you would never have let him go. Better that those of us who took the cut return it all to you. As the saying goes: when hero meets hero, a knocked-out tooth is swallowed and done with." E said, "Since the company is returning the cut, I too will give back three taels for the show and add one tael more for the treat. From it, take five qian, exchange it for a thread of gold, and have a ring made for Brother Xu as a warning against gambling—for 'ring' and 'warning' share the same character." The company all said, "Brother Zhang's words are most reasonable. This is a hero cherishing a hero, a truly generous man." Huasheng fell silent. Truly it is said: keep to your lot and covet nothing, and no one can lure you; let greed sprout within, and ruin is sure to follow.

Note: Gamblers falling into snares suffer far worse fates than this. E, being a wealthy merchant with capital, was not cleaned out entirely; he handled the conclusion skillfully, leaving a warning for others. Had it been a sharp con man in a gambling den, what care would he have for your ten-thousand-tael fortune? Every last coin would have fallen into his hands. Let those who come after look at Xu Huasheng, who lost everything and repented too late—take warning and do not tread the same path.
